title: AI enters clinical evidence workflows
evidence: ASHG paired AI-enhanced multiomic tools, best practices for AI in variant interpretation, and agentic reasoning across genome, RNA, and phenotype data.
implication: Competitive advantage is shifting from model access to evidence integration, calibration, and auditable interpretation.
action: Convene an evaluation-focused CABS roundtable across developers, labs, and clinicians.

title: Sequence models face a trust threshold
evidence: The program highlighted sequence-to-function models, independent CAGI evaluation, confidence signals, and gene/domain-aware calibration.
implication: Model ranking alone is insufficient; validation design and calibrated uncertainty are becoming adoption gates.
action: Create a practical scorecard for evaluating genomic foundation models.

title: Knowledge graphs become connective tissue
evidence: A featured symposium covered AI and knowledge graphs across the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem, including Bridge2AI and the Data Distillery Knowledge Graph.
implication: Structured connectivity across datasets and mechanisms may matter as much as larger standalone models.
action: Map CABS data-science expertise to interoperable knowledge-graph use cases.

title: Long reads move from edge to clinic
evidence: A highlighted platform session traced long-read genomics from biobanks to clinical use; multiple talks paired long reads with methylation and RNA analysis.
implication: Long-read adoption is becoming a workflow and reimbursement question, not just a technical feasibility question.
action: Develop a member primer on validated clinical use cases and operational barriers.
session: The Long and Short of It

title: Isoform resolution becomes a biology layer
evidence: ASHG highlighted a platform session on moving from gene-level analyses to isoform-resolved biology, alongside long-read RNA sequencing and splicing studies.
implication: Gene-level summaries may increasingly miss actionable disease mechanisms and therapeutic hypotheses.
action: Track tools that connect isoform evidence to target and biomarker decisions.

title: Multi-omics becomes ancestry-aware
evidence: The GenomeCast program featured MAMO: Multi-Ancestry-Aware Multi-Omics Analysis for Complex Diseases, while the broader program repeatedly integrated single-cell, proteomic, epigenomic, and spatial data.
implication: Integration methods must handle ancestry and context explicitly to avoid scaling bias with data volume.
action: Prioritize cross-population validation in CABS multi-omics programming.

title: Human genetics tightens target selection
evidence: A featured symposium covered translation of human genetics into therapeutic targets and clinical development, including prioritization frameworks and trial prediction.
implication: Genetic evidence is moving closer to portfolio selection and development strategy, with explicit calibration of causal confidence.
action: Build a CABS case-study series linking genetic evidence to program decisions.

title: Rare disease scales through combined evidence
evidence: Sessions combined automated genome interpretation, transcriptomics, functional assays, population cohorts, and multi-omic diagnostics for unsolved disease.
implication: Diagnostic lift will come from orchestrated evidence layers and reanalysis, not sequencing alone.
action: Compare end-to-end diagnostic workflows rather than individual tools.

title: Population screening shifts to implementation
evidence: A featured symposium moved adult DNA-based population screening from pilots to practice, covering actionability, service scaling, and a 14,000-participant implementation pilot.
implication: Evidence, service capacity, and follow-up pathways are converging into one implementation problem.
action: Surface operating models and outcome measures for responsible genomic screening.

title: Gene therapy scale depends on policy
evidence: A dedicated session addressed policy pathways for safe, scalable gene-therapy innovation.
implication: Manufacturing and scientific progress must be matched by regulatory, access, and governance pathways.
action: Pair scientific updates with policy and access voices in CABS events.

title: Public trust is treated as infrastructure
evidence: The Presidential Symposium focused on evidence, storytelling, and public trust, while another session addressed ethical and cultural implications of genomics research.
implication: Communication quality and community legitimacy are operational requirements for genomic programs.
action: Add trust, communication, and community engagement criteria to program planning.

title: Global genomics emphasizes implementation
evidence: The distinguished symposium framed global human genetics from discovery through implementation; sessions also covered African rare disease, diverse biobanks, and representation gaps.
implication: Equity is increasingly linked to infrastructure, local delivery, and analytical validity—not representation counts alone.
action: Feature implementation partnerships with local leadership and durable capacity.
